solution: Here \(a = 7 > 0\) and \(b = -5 < 0\), so the point lies in the fourth quadrant. \(|z| = \sqrt{7^2+(-5)^2} = \sqrt{49+25} = \sqrt{74}\), and \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{-5}{7}\). \(\therefore\) modulus \(= \sqrt{74}\) and amplitude \(= -\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{7}\right)\), equivalently \(2\pi - \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{5}{7}\right)\).

Here \(a = \sqrt{3} > 0\) and \(b = \sqrt{2} > 0\), so the point lies in the first quadrant. \(|z| = \sqrt{(\sqrt{3})^2+(\sqrt{2})^2} = \sqrt{3+2} = \sqrt{5}\), and \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}\). \(\therefore\) modulus \(= \sqrt{5}\) and amplitude \(= \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\).
_note: [Textbook misprint in the printed key (modulus only): where the modulus should stand, the key prints a lone bold italic letter \(i\). Checked at high zoom on the answer page — the glyph is an italic i, not a radical. The modulus of \(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2}\,i\) is \(\sqrt{3+2} = \sqrt{5}\); a modulus is a non-negative real number and can never be \(i\). The amplitude printed alongside it is correct.]

solution: Here \(a = -8 < 0\) and \(b = 15 > 0\), so the point lies in the second quadrant. \(|z| = \sqrt{(-8)^2+15^2} = \sqrt{64+225} = \sqrt{289} = 17\). In the second quadrant the amplitude is \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right) + \pi = -\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{15}{8}\right) + \pi\). \(\therefore\) modulus \(= 17\) and amplitude \(= \pi - \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{15}{8}\right)\).
_note: [Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives the amplitude as \(-\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{15}{8}\right)\), dropping the quadrant term. That angle is negative and so points into the FOURTH quadrant, whereas \(-8+15i\) lies in the SECOND — the two directions differ by \(\pi\). The chapter's own table in section 1.5.3 states the rule for \(a<0, b>0\) as \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)+\pi\) with \(\frac{\pi}{2} < \theta < \pi\), which gives \(\pi - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{15}{8}\right) \approx 2.06\) radians. The modulus \(17\) is correct. The identical slip appears in the key for sub-item v), so this is not an isolated typo.]

solution: Here \(-3(1-i) = -3+3i\), so \(a = -3 < 0\) and \(b = 3 > 0\) and the point lies in the second quadrant. \(|z| = \sqrt{9+9} = 3\sqrt{2}\), and the amplitude is \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{-3}\right) + \pi = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \pi\). \(\therefore\) modulus \(= 3\sqrt{2}\) and amplitude \(= \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\).

Here \(a = -4 < 0\) and \(b = -4 < 0\), so the point lies in the third quadrant. \(|z| = \sqrt{16+16} = 4\sqrt{2}\). In the third quadrant the amplitude is \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{-4}{-4}\right) + \pi = \dfrac{\pi}{4} + \pi\). \(\therefore\) modulus \(= 4\sqrt{2}\) and amplitude \(= \dfrac{5\pi}{4}\), equivalently \(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\).
_note: [Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives the amplitude as \(\frac{\pi}{4}\), which is the bare \(\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)\) with the quadrant term omitted. \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) points into the FIRST quadrant, whereas \(-4-4i\) lies in the THIRD; the two directions differ by \(\pi\). The chapter's own table in section 1.5.3 states the rule for \(a<0, b<0\) as \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)+\pi\) with \(\pi < \theta < \frac{3\pi}{2}\), giving \(\frac{5\pi}{4}\). The modulus \(4\sqrt{2}\) is correct. The same omission appears in the key for sub-item iii).]

solution: Here \(a = \sqrt{3} > 0\) and \(b = -1 < 0\), so the point lies in the fourth quadrant. \(|z| = \sqrt{3+1} = 2\). In the fourth quadrant the amplitude is \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{-1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) + 2\pi = -\dfrac{\pi}{6} + 2\pi\). \(\therefore\) modulus \(= 2\) and amplitude \(= \dfrac{11\pi}{6}\), equivalently \(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\).
_note: [Textbook answer-key omission: the printed key gives only the amplitude \(\frac{11\pi}{6}\) for this item and prints no modulus at all, although the question asks for both and every other sub-item of Q.1 carries the pair. The missing modulus is \(2\). The amplitude printed is correct.]

solution: Here \(z = 3 + 0i\), so \(a = 3 > 0\) and \(b = 0\): the point lies on the positive real axis. \(|z| = \sqrt{3^2+0^2} = 3\) and \(\theta = 0\). \(\therefore\) modulus \(= 3\) and amplitude \(= 0\).

Here \(a = 1 > 0\) and \(b = 1 > 0\), so the point lies in the first quadrant. \(|z| = \sqrt{1+1} = \sqrt{2}\) and the amplitude is \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{1}\right) = \tan^{-1}(1)\). \(\therefore\) modulus \(= \sqrt{2}\) and amplitude \(= \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

Here \(a = 1 > 0\) and \(b = \sqrt{3} > 0\), so the point lies in the first quadrant. \(|z| = \sqrt{1+3} = 2\) and the amplitude is \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{1}\right) = \tan^{-1}(\sqrt{3})\). \(\therefore\) modulus \(= 2\) and amplitude \(= \dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

First simplify: \((1+2i)^2 = 1+4i-4 = -3+4i\), so \((1+2i)^2(1-i) = (-3+4i)(1-i) = -3+3i+4i+4 = 1+7i\). Here \(a = 1 > 0\) and \(b = 7 > 0\), so the point lies in the first quadrant. \(|z| = \sqrt{1+49} = \sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}\) and the amplitude is \(\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{7}{1}\right)\). \(\therefore\) modulus \(= 5\sqrt{2}\) and amplitude \(= \tan^{-1}(7)\).

Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator: \(\dfrac{(4+3i\sin\theta)(1+2i\sin\theta)}{(1-2i\sin\theta)(1+2i\sin\theta)} = \dfrac{4 - 6\sin^2\theta + 11i\sin\theta}{1+4\sin^2\theta}\). The number is purely real when its imaginary part vanishes, and since \(1+4\sin^2\theta \ne 0\) this needs \(11\sin\theta = 0\), i.e. \(\sin\theta = 0\). \(\therefore \theta = n\pi\), \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\)

With \(z = 3+5i\) we get \(\overline{z} = 3-5i\), \(-z = -3-5i\) and \(-\overline{z} = -3+5i\). On the Argand diagram these are plotted as the points \(P(3,\,5)\), \(Q(3,\,-5)\), \(R(-3,\,-5)\) and \(S(-3,\,5)\) respectively. \(Q\) is the reflection of \(P\) in the X-axis, \(S\) is the reflection of \(P\) in the Y-axis, and \(R\) is the reflection of \(P\) in the origin. \(\therefore\) the four points are the vertices of a rectangle of sides \(6\) and \(10\) units centred at the origin.
diagramNote: Argand diagram: X-axis (real) and Y-axis (imaginary) through the origin, scale about -6 to 6 horizontally and -6 to 6 vertically. Plot and label four points: P(3, 5) marked z, Q(3, -5) marked z-conjugate, R(-3, -5) marked -z, S(-3, 5) marked -z-conjugate. Optionally join P-Q-R-S to show the rectangle centred at the origin.

solution: Here \(a = -1\), \(b = \sqrt{3}\), so \(r = \sqrt{1+3} = 2\) and the point lies in the second quadrant, giving \(\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{-1}\right) + \pi = -\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \pi = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). \(\therefore -1+\sqrt{3}\,i = 2\left(\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} + i\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right) = 2e^{\frac{2\pi}{3}i}\)

Here \(a = 0\), \(b = -1\), so \(r = \sqrt{0+1} = 1\) and the point lies on the negative imaginary axis, giving \(\theta = \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\). \(\therefore -i = 1\left(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + i\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right) = e^{\frac{3\pi}{2}i}\)
Here \(a = -1\), \(b = 0\), so \(r = \sqrt{1+0} = 1\) and the point lies on the negative real axis, giving \(\theta = \pi\). \(\therefore -1 = 1(\cos\pi + i\sin\pi) = e^{\pi i}\)

First \(\dfrac{1}{1+i} = \dfrac{1-i}{(1+i)(1-i)} = \dfrac{1-i}{2}\), so \(a = \dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(b = -\dfrac{1}{2}\). Then \(r = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), and the point lies in the fourth quadrant, so \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(-1) + 2\pi = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} + 2\pi = \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\). \(\therefore \dfrac{1}{1+i} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4} + i\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{\frac{7\pi}{4}i}\)

First \(\dfrac{1+2i}{1-3i} = \dfrac{(1+2i)(1+3i)}{1+9} = \dfrac{1+3i+2i-6}{10} = \dfrac{-5+5i}{10} = \dfrac{-1+i}{2}\), so \(a = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(b = \dfrac{1}{2}\). Then \(r = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), and the point lies in the second quadrant, so \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(-1) + \pi = -\dfrac{\pi}{4} + \pi = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\). \(\therefore \dfrac{1+2i}{1-3i} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{4} + i\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}e^{\frac{3\pi}{4}i}\)

Here \((2-i)^2 = 4-4i-1 = 3-4i\), so \(\dfrac{1+7i}{(2-i)^2} = \dfrac{(1+7i)(3+4i)}{9+16} = \dfrac{3+4i+21i-28}{25} = \dfrac{-25+25i}{25} = -1+i\). Then \(r = \sqrt{1+1} = \sqrt{2}\), and the point lies in the second quadrant, so \(\theta = \tan^{-1}(-1) + \pi = \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\). \(\therefore \dfrac{1+7i}{(2-i)^2} = \sqrt{2}\left(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{4} + i\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right) = \sqrt{2}\,e^{\frac{3\pi}{4}i}\)

Substituting \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}\): \(\sqrt{3}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}i\right) = \dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i\). \(\therefore\) the number is \(\dfrac{3}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\)

Substituting \(\cos\dfrac{7\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and \(\sin\dfrac{7\pi}{4} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\): \(\sqrt{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}i\right) = 1 - i\). \(\therefore\) the number is \(1-i\)

Substituting \(\cos\left(-\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(\sin\left(-\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) = -\dfrac{1}{2}\): \(7\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}i\right) = -\dfrac{7\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{7}{2}i\). \(\therefore\) the number is \(-\dfrac{7\sqrt{3}}{2} - \dfrac{7i}{2}\)

By Euler's formula \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\), so \(e^{\frac{\pi}{3}i} = \cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} + i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}i\). \(\therefore\) the number is \(\dfrac{1+\sqrt{3}\,i}{2}\)

By Euler's formula, \(e^{\frac{-4\pi}{3}i} = \cos\left(-\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) + i\sin\left(-\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3} - i\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3} = -\dfrac{1}{2} - i\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\). \(\therefore\) the number is \(\dfrac{-1+i\sqrt{3}}{2}\)
By Euler's formula, \(e^{\frac{5\pi}{6}i} = \cos\dfrac{5\pi}{6} + i\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{6} = -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2}i\). \(\therefore\) the number is \(\dfrac{-\sqrt{3}+i}{2}\)

First simplify: \(\dfrac{1+2i}{1-3i} = \dfrac{(1+2i)(1+3i)}{1+9} = \dfrac{1+3i+2i-6}{10} = \dfrac{-5+5i}{10} = \dfrac{-1+i}{2}\). Here \(a = -\dfrac{1}{2}\) and \(b = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(|z| = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{4}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\), and the point lies in the second quadrant, so \(\arg z = \tan^{-1}(-1) + \pi = -\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\pi\). \(\therefore\) modulus \(= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\) and argument \(= \dfrac{3\pi}{4}\).

The numerator \(i-1 = -1+i\) has modulus \(\sqrt{2}\) and, lying in the second quadrant, argument \(\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\). The denominator \(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3} + i\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) has modulus \(1\) and argument \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\). On division the moduli divide and the arguments subtract, so \(|z| = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{1} = \sqrt{2}\) and \(\arg z = \dfrac{3\pi}{4} - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{9\pi-4\pi}{12} = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}\). \(\therefore z = \sqrt{2}\left(\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{12} + i\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{12}\right)\)

For \(z = 2+3i\) we have \(\overline{z} = 2-3i\). Taking the conjugate again reverses the sign of the imaginary part once more: \(\overline{(\overline{z})} = \overline{2-3i} = 2+3i\), which is \(z\). \(\therefore \overline{(\overline{z})} = z\) is verified.

Here \(z\,\overline{z} = (2+3i)(2-3i) = 4 - 9i^2 = 4+9 = 13\). Also \(|z| = \sqrt{2^2+3^2} = \sqrt{13}\), so \(|z|^2 = 13\). Both sides equal \(13\). \(\therefore z\,\overline{z} = |z|^2\) is verified.
Here \(z + \overline{z} = (2+3i) + (2-3i) = 4 + 0i\). Its imaginary part is zero, so it is a real number. \(\therefore (z+\overline{z}) = 4\) is real, which is verified.
Here \(z - \overline{z} = (2+3i) - (2-3i) = 2+3i-2+3i = 6i\). \(\therefore z - \overline{z} = 6i\) is verified.

L.H.S.: \(z_1 + z_2 = (1+i)+(2-3i) = 3-2i\), so \(\overline{z_1+z_2} = 3+2i\). R.H.S.: \(\overline{z_1} + \overline{z_2} = (1-i)+(2+3i) = 3+2i\). Both sides equal \(3+2i\). \(\therefore \overline{z_1+z_2} = \overline{z_1}+\overline{z_2}\) is verified.

L.H.S.: \(z_1 - z_2 = (1+i)-(2-3i) = -1+4i\), so \(\overline{z_1-z_2} = -1-4i\). R.H.S.: \(\overline{z_1} - \overline{z_2} = (1-i)-(2+3i) = -1-4i\). Both sides equal \(-1-4i\). \(\therefore \overline{z_1-z_2} = \overline{z_1}-\overline{z_2}\) is verified.

L.H.S.: \(z_1 z_2 = (1+i)(2-3i) = 2-3i+2i+3 = 5-i\), so \(\overline{z_1 \cdot z_2} = 5+i\). R.H.S.: \(\overline{z_1}\cdot\overline{z_2} = (1-i)(2+3i) = 2+3i-2i+3 = 5+i\). Both sides equal \(5+i\). \(\therefore \overline{z_1 \cdot z_2} = \overline{z_1}\cdot\overline{z_2}\) is verified.

L.H.S.: \(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2} = \dfrac{1+i}{2-3i} = \dfrac{(1+i)(2+3i)}{4+9} = \dfrac{2+3i+2i-3}{13} = \dfrac{-1+5i}{13}\), so its conjugate is \(\dfrac{-1-5i}{13}\). R.H.S.: \(\dfrac{\overline{z_1}}{\overline{z_2}} = \dfrac{1-i}{2+3i} = \dfrac{(1-i)(2-3i)}{4+9} = \dfrac{2-3i-2i-3}{13} = \dfrac{-1-5i}{13}\). Both sides equal \(\dfrac{-1-5i}{13}\). \(\therefore \overline{\left(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\right)} = \dfrac{\overline{z_1}}{\overline{z_2}}\) is verified.
